en: The Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra is completed. This manuscript belongs to the alms-gathering monk Śīlākaragupta.
[1] Homage to Bhūtaḍāmara!

Resembling the clouds at the end of an aeon, with a most deformed face, emitting terrifying loud laughs, his limbs enveloped in garlands of flames, with his lotus-feet placed upon the head of the enemy of Tripura,
being praised by divine beings, wielding a blazing thunderbolt, and threatening with wrath—
Having bowed to that Lord of Beings, I shall describe his mandala as taught by my spiritual preceptors.

In this regard, first, the Master— possessing the resolve to uplift the entire world, having purified all objects of experience through the realization of the natural luminosity attained by the power of faith, learning, and so forth, firm in purity, and acting with the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of negating [obstructions] within the omnipresent *dharmadhātu*— having removed the veil of delusion by shaking off the latencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization through the increase of the equipment of wisdom, should, when requested by the disciple two or three times to draw the mandala, ask: "Are all your necessary materials complete or not?"
If he should say that something is accomplished while something else is not,

then one should imagine a stake (*kīlaka*) arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*, having the form of a wrathful deity at its upper end and the shape of a trident at its lower end; with this, one should pin down the obstacles to his mind, incinerate the wicked with its thousands of terrifying rays, and for the protection of the disciple’s mind, contemplate a moon disc born from the letter *A* and the Action-Vajra (*karmavajra*) situated therein, which has arisen from the final vowel.

Then, having gathered companions who have seen the maṇḍala, who possess faith, have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), are knowledgeable in the procedures of the secret method, maintain pure and clean conduct, are skilled in the performance of protective rites, are resolute, and possess stable intellects, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) in a place agreeable to the mind, such as a mountain, forest, riverbank, garden, or dwelling.

Then, having consecrated the water for the guest-offering (argha) with the four-syllable mantra and the syllable HŪṂ, one should cause the Blessed One’s form residing in the cloth or other support to descend, worship him with external and internal offerings such as incense and so forth, and perform the confession of sins and other rites.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; and I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.

Then, having visualized an eight-petaled lotus at the throat by means of the syllable *hrīḥ*, and a white vajra upon the petal of the tongue-lotus by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one consecrates it as the "Vajra-Tongue. Then, having meditated on a moon-maṇḍala in both hands by means of the syllable *aṃ*, and the blazing syllable *dhūṃ* above it—which is a wheel of flames—one should speak thus while forming the hollowed-añjali gesture:
Oṃ Siddhicakra Hūṃ.
Then one should perform the protection of the site.

One should utter the syllable *hūṃ*. Instantly manifesting oneself as the King of Wrath (*Krodharāja*), and having visualized the Destroyer of All Obstacles (*Sarvavighnāntaka*)—produced from the syllable *hūṃ*, shaped like a spike below the navel and having the form of a wrathful deity above, terrifying with thousands of flames—one should look down at the obstacles and, while reciting the mantra, drive them into the earth, pinning them down as far as the bottomless abyss (*ārasātala*).
Oṃ gha gha, slay, slay all malevolent ones, phaṭ! Stake, stake all sins, phaṭ! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Vajrakīla, the Holder of the Vajra commands: stake the body, speech, and mind! Hūṃ phaṭ!
In front of that, one should visualize a solar disc blazing with rays, born from the syllable *Āṃ*. One should contemplate stakes with flaming rays in all directions;
by means of these, one's own self is enclosed within a cage bound together on all sides.
In the vajra-binding, with the thumbs joined and the index fingers bent and held upon one's own lap—
this mudrā bestows all accomplishments.
Oṃ, you who are born from the nature of all completely pure phenomena, be accomplished! Hūṃ!
One should recite [the mantra] seven times.

Then, having visualized a moon by means of the syllable *Ā* in the heart and, upon it, the syllable *Raṃ* like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kalpāgni*), one should clasp the fingers together, extend the two index fingers, and purify the evil by starting from the forehead with the yoga of "bursting open" the evil.
Oṃ, strike, destroy, annihilate evil! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Having thus burned away the self, together with its external and internal aspects, and having burst asunder the evils of conceptual construction, one should contemplate [the mind] as being like the sky, liberated from the grasped and the grasper.
Then, the mind— shaken free of conceptualization, self-cognizable, and luminous— [arises].
Interspersed with the syllables *hūṃ* and *hoḥ*, which produce bliss,
one should gladden the realm of sentient beings— which is manifested as mind-only— and then bring it to unity with one’s own mind by means of the masses of rays produced from that [mind].
Then one should see [it] like a reflection, joined with the half-moon and the bindu.

Then, by means of the vowels beginning with *a*, one should emit a circle; having caused the short vowels—which are of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*)—and the long ones—which are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*)—to emerge, one should make the mind free from them. Then, one should contemplate those [vowels] as white, entering again through the very mouth of the rays, starting from the lineage (*gotra*). And the body should likewise be contemplated in this same manner, in the form of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*).
Then, having emanated Buddhas of five colors and caused them to enter, one should visualize oneself as the Great Being (Mahāsattva) upon a white lotus with rays of light.

Above that, one should meditate on oneself as the syllable *HŪṂ*, from which arises a black flaming vajra. Having emanated the Family of Wrath (*krodhakula*) and causing it to enter, one should speak thus while binding the wrathful possession (*krodhāveśa*).
Oṃ krodhāveśa hūṃ 3 aḥ || Mantra ||
In this regard, the following is the manifestation of anger:

Forming a mutual fist, one should encircle the two index fingers; this is the *krodhāveśā* [mudrā]. Then, the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) should be performed with the thought, "I am Krodhavajra. Thereafter, having again projected and re-absorbed the *krodhakula*, one should generate the firm conviction: "I am Śrī Bhūtaḍāmara."
Oṃ, O Vajra-possessor, cause [them] to enter; cause [them] to fall! Hūṃ!
Just as the possession by wrathful deities is joined with mantra, so too is the possession by Vajra.
Then, having resolved "I am the Wrathful Vajra," and having bound the pledge-seal (samayamudrā), one thinks, "I am the pledge."
Having empowered one's own [body] through the commitment (*samaya*),
one should say "Āḥ.
One should encircle with the two ring fingers and bend the two index fingers.
One should press the little finger and the middle finger with the thumb.
Its mantra is: HŪṂ VAJRA PHAṬ.
Having placed [the mudrā] on the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head, one should preside over them.
Then, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with their respective mudrās and mantras.
Having formed the mutual fist, one should extend the middle fingers.
The mantra of the head-seal.
Oṃ hana vajra hūṃ.
The head.
Having inserted the two middle fingers of this very [hand] and formed the index fingers into a needle, this is the mantra for the crest-lock mudrā (śikhāmudrā).
Oṃ, burn, vajra, hūṃ!
The crest [mudrā]: from this same mudrā, with the two thumbs at the sides—the right thumb on the right side and the left thumb on the left side—it is the eye-mudrā.
Oṃ dīptavajra hūṃ.
The eye-mantra.
Forming a mutual fist, one should interlace the two little fingers and extend the index fingers;
this is the heart mudrā mantra.
Having placed the wrathful vajra empowered by the syllable HŪṂ at his heart.
Oṃ vajrarosha hūṃ.
The heart.
Having formed the index finger of this very same mudrā into a coil, it is the mantra of the armor mudrā.
Oṃ, firm armor, [svāhā].
The Armor.
Extending both index fingers of this very same mudrā is the mantra of the weapon-mudrā (astramudrā).
Mantra: Oṃ hana daha paca krodhavajra sarvaduṣṭān māraya hūṃ phaṭ.

Having recited the mantra of the weapon three times while uttering "hūṃ āḥ," one should place a blue wrathful vajra upon a moon mandala in front; then, saying "I am the vajra," and through its transformation, one should meditate on the wrathful deity, thinking "I am the wrathful one.
Thereafter, one should invoke the Blessed One.
Having placed them so that they mutually interlock and having bent the two index fingers,
the wise one should slightly move the two thumbs and draw them toward himself with the index fingers.
Its mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, Vajradhara, great wrathful one, protect the samaya; come quickly! Hrīḥ jaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Having thus drawn [the deity] forward, caused the *jñānasattva* to enter, bound it, and brought it under control, one should praise it with this: "O Great King, accomplished in wrath, in the teaching of the *siddhi-samaya*,
may all the gods be successful and swiftly attain unsurpassed accomplishment."
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, you who grant accomplishment at that very moment— O Siddhivajra, Great Wrathful One, abide as the deity of the pledge!
Homage be to you, homage be to you, homage be to you, homage again and again!
I am your devotee; I take refuge in you. O Bhūtaḍāmara, grant me success!
Then, the removal of obstacles should be performed with this:
*Oṃ nāśaya sarvaduṣṭān daha paca bhasmīkuru hūṃ 3 phaṭ 3*. This is the mantra.
Its mudrā is as follows: having formed two fists with the hands, one should extend the two thumbs;
with this, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
Oṃ vajrakrodha mahācaṇḍa, bind the ten directions! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Its mudrā is as follows:

having formed two separate fists with the hands, one should extend the two thumbs. Extending the left index finger, one should place it at the base of the arm. Pressing the nail of the little finger with the right thumb, one should extend the remaining fingers and place them at the base of the arm; then, being wrathful, one should whirl [the hand] through the ten directions and suddenly cast it down and up.
With the vajra-gaze, one should create a protective enclosure and cage.
Then one should offer the *argha* water.

When available, having placed barley and milk along with fragrant water and the like into an *argha* vessel made of gold, silver, copper, stone, wood, clay, conch shell, mother-of-pearl, or a leaf-cup, one should worship it.
Oṃ! All deities, be gracious; O Blessed One, Great Wrathful One, accept this water offering, hūṃ aḥ!
The mantra.
Its mudrā is as follows.
Having formed the *añjali* with the palms facing upward and the two thumbs placed on the sides,
one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the feet with this very [gesture].
Then, having bound the *samayāgrī* [mudrā], one should display the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*).
HŪṂ VAJRA PHAṬ! The visible world: JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ!
One should cause it to enter one's own body;
from behind, one should enter the sun.
"You are the pledge, you are the pledge; I am HŪṂ VAJRA PHAṬ."
Thus one should recite three times.

Then, one should visualize oneself as [the deity] surrounded by a mass of blazing flames, with a luster like crushed collyrium, possessing a fierce gaze, adorned with a garland of skulls, having a face formidable with fangs, and emitting a loud, boisterous laugh. He has four arms: with the right, he brandishes a blue wrathful-vajra; with the left, he threatens the wicked; with two hands at his heart, he holds the mudrā and carries a vajra-bell; and he is adorned with ornaments of serpents. One should contemplate him thus.

Now follow the description of the abodes and ornaments of the *nāgas*. Karkoṭaka is blue and wears a turban; Nanda and Upananda are yellow and serve as earrings; Ananta and Vāsuki are white and serve as the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and the waist-band (*kaṭisūtra*).

On his two right arms are bracelets made of the serpents Kulika and Pārāvata, which are yellow; on his [two] breasts are Śaṅkhapāla, who is white; and Padma and Mahāpadma, who are red and serve as anklets.
They have spread out the expansion of their hoods and are exhaling the fire of poison.
One should contemplate those highly fortunate ones who are agitated by the eight kinds of poison.

He should then offer them a seat. Having turned the left hand palm upward, one should grasp the left thumb with the right fist, with the thumb of the right hand raised; this is the Bhūtāsana-mudrā of Vajradhara.
Oṃ jaya 2! O Great Lord of Wrath, King of Great Wrath! Show this seat of spirits! Protect! Seize! Svāhā!
One should visualize the unconquerable being as having stepped upon [the enemy].

One should visualize the unconquerable great being as three-eyed, pot-bellied, four-armed, fanged, and tawny; consecrated by the white-colored [deity] with tawny matted hair and the half-moon; wearing a garland of skulls, fierce, with a snake as a sacred thread, and clad in half a tiger skin; adorned with tawny beard and mustache; holding a *gaṇetṛ* (or *gaṇeśvara*) and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) in his two right hands, and holding a skull-cup and a trident in his two left hands.
Then, with a wrathful gaze, one should place the syllable *hār* on the eyes and apply the root mantra to the mouth.

Then, having visualized a flaming vajra at one’s own heart by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should bind the *samayāgra* as before. One should place the syllable *hūṃ* on the tongue as previously described; this is the *dharmamudrā*. Having meditated upon a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) at the heart by means of the syllable *aḥ*, the *mahāmudrā* is joined with the mantra.
Thus, the *karmamudrā* is devoid of such symbols. Having visualized a wrathful vajra at the heart by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, the *mahāmudrā* follows the [prescribed] drawing.
Then, by means of the *siddhivajrākarṣaṇamudrā*, one should draw the Blessed One into one’s own body and cause him to enter.
With this mudrā-mantra:
having formed two fists with the hands, one should wrap both little fingers around and extend the index fingers to form the shape of a hook.
This is the *siddhi*-mudrā for summoning.
The mantra.
Oṃ vajra-roṣa mahākrodha, quickly summon! Hūṃ jaḥ!
Then, having likewise empowered [the disciple] with the samaya-mudrā, one should recite one’s own mantra three times. One should receive the empowerment with:
*oṃ vajrābhiṣiñca*.
Taking scented water from a flask empowered by the Vajra with the Krodhamuṣṭi [mudrā], one should consecrate oneself.

Then, having empowered the crown of skulls produced from the syllable *hūṃ* by means of that very [mantra], and having bound the *vajra-terittirī* [mudrā] for the consecration with the *vajra-mālā*, one should take hold of it.
This is as follows: in the *vajra-bandha*, one should extend both thumbs and hold the *vajra-muṣṭi* at the head.
Again, the consecration with the garland of skulls is performed with this [mantra].
Hūṃ. Now follows the mudrā.
With all the fingers joined at their bases and all the tips joined at their ends,
it is covered by the vajra of the thumbs, reaching to the hollows of the nose and eyes.

Having visualized five skull-cups on this [deity’s] head—on the forehead, the right ear, the back of the head, and above the left ear—one should then perform the consecration of the Tathāgata crown with these [syllables]:
ĀḤ HŪṂ TRĪḤ HRĪḤ AḤ. Having thus accomplished the consecration of the body by the Tathāgatas, that [consecration] arises from the vajra-añjali.

With the thumb acting as the central being in the paryaṅka posture, its tip slightly curved, the body upright, the middle and upper parts level, and the remaining fingers possessing the luster of the vajrāñjali—
this is the mantra.
"Oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ, consecrate me!
Thus, one should visualize Vairocana, with a golden luster, situated at the crown of the head in the position of the *bodhyagra*.
Likewise: Vajrasattva hūṃ; Vajraratna trāṃ; Vajradharma hrīḥ; Vajrakarma aḥ.
Thus, "Sprinkle me" is [recited] everywhere.

Upon the forehead, the right ear, the head, the back, and the left ear, there are white, green, red, and variegated-colored Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, established with the earth-touching, boon-granting, meditative equipoise, and fear-dispelling mudrās respectively. They are of the nature of Amitābha and the five Tathāgatas; they should be visualized as abiding through the yoga of the crown.

Then, having performed the armor-protection once with both index fingers while reciting *oṃ* and *huṃ*, one should satisfy [the deity] with equanimity by reciting *oṃ vajra tuṣya hoḥ* while the rosary is joined in the manner of a sash and the last bead is released from the first. Having uttered the hundred-syllable mantra, one should take hold of the vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ* with this [mantra].
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration;
take this state of omnibuddhahood, O Vajra, for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; remain, O Vajra, you are the Samaya.

With this, having placed that vajra upon the head [of the disciple] with the words "Oṃ, may Vajrapāṇi arise as the performer of vajra-activities," one should receive the name-consecration (nāmābhiṣeka), beginning with:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as Vajrakrodha through the name-consecration of 'Vajra'; O Śrī Krodhavajra! and so forth.
Then one should take up the vajra-vow.
This is that state of all buddhahood, residing in the hand of Vajrasattva;
you too must always uphold it, O Vajrapāṇi of firm vows.
"Oṃ, O Vajra-samaya of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, abide! I uphold you, O Vajrasattva, hrīḥ hi 4 hūṃ.

Then, having performed worship according to the method to be described, having made it firm with the hundred-syllable mantra, and having bound the Blessed One’s mahāmudrā, one should grasp the vajra as the reality (tattva).
"Krodhavajrasattva, who arises from passion, is to be tamed;
I am indeed the supreme dissolution, like the sun amidst the fire of vajra-flames.
This is the reality (*tattva*).
One should ring the bell produced from the syllable *Aḥ*:
"Everything has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics;
one who is united with the equality of space shall quickly accomplish everything."
Such is the Dharma. One should consecrate the Mahāmudrā by means of the pledge (samaya),
saying "the entire sky" through the yoga of the supreme of all skies.
Sealed by the vajra-mudrās, one may even consume the three worlds; such is the samaya.

Then, abiding in the Mahāmudrā within the space of the intellect, one should utter the syllable *HŪṂ* and visualize all Buddha-fields as equal to the sky. In that space of the sky, by means of the syllable *YAṂ*, one visualizes a wind-maṇḍala; above that, by means of the syllable *VAṂ*, a water-maṇḍala; again, above that, by means of the syllable *LAṂ*, a golden maṇḍala; and again, above that, by means of the syllable *VAṂ*, a great ocean. There, upon the water and golden maṇḍalas, one contemplates the four-sided Great Meru, adorned with all jewels and composed of the four precious gems, [visualized] by means of the syllables *HŪṂ SUṂ HŪṂ*.

Having empowered [the site] with "HŪṂ" and having emanated a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) endowed with square and other features by means of that very syllable HŪṂ, one should visualize within its center the elephant-throne with "HŪṂ GAṂ HŪṂ," which is occupied by a lotus and moon-maṇḍala arising from the syllable HŪṂ. Having descended and remained there in the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), one should then summon the unconquerable great spirit (aparājita-mahābhūta), together with Mahādeva and others, by means of the previously mentioned mantra and mudrā for invocation.
Then, having bound the Great Seal of the Blessed One, [one recites]:
"OṂ VAJRAJVĀLE HANA 2 SARVABHŪTĀN HŪṂ PHAṬ."
One should contemplate that [the deceased] has been dried up and rendered dead by the Blessed One’s Vajrajvālā.
"Oṃ vajrāyuṣe sara 2 smiṃ!
O Blessed One, may he be revived once again by these [rays] called the 'Revivifier of the Dead,' which are the great winds issued forth from the nostrils."

"Oṃ hana 2 sarvān māraya vajrajvālena hūṃ phaṭ. Having filled the entire realm of space with this vajra-flame, one should slay Mahādeva and all other gods—excluding Aparājita, whom it cannot dry up—with this mantra: "Hūṃ hana phaṭ! One should thus slay Mahādeva and all the other deities.
Furthermore, one may restore all of them to life by means of this mantra.
Oṃ kaḍḍha 2, restore the dead to life! Hrīḥ Aḥ!
Then, having formed the *saṃpuṭāñjali* mudrā opened in the shape of a lotus, one should offer a seat to the Blessed One and to the gods and others with the mantra:
*oṃ padmodbhavaniṣaṇṇāya sarvadevatā svāhā*.
One should visualize the unconquerable great element as being stepped upon as before by the previously mentioned seat-mantra and mudrā.
Having removed all suffering through an intention of loving-kindness (*maitryāśaya*), one should establish Mahādeva and the others by their very names.
Having established them, they should be marked with the four seals (*caturmudrāmudrita*).
In this regard, there is the following rule concerning their positions, seats, and colors.

In the east is Maheśvara, mounted on a bull, ash-colored, wearing a snake as a sacred thread, three-eyed, consecrated with the crescent moon, and possessing an erect liṅga. He holds a *gaṇetṛ* and a *ḍamaru* drum in his two right hands, and a skull-cup and a trident in his two left hands.
Having formed the *añjali* gesture with palms facing upward, one should bend the index and ring fingers.
This is the *triśūla-mudrā*. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
To the right of Mahādeva is Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa, wearing a jewel crown and mounted upon Garuḍa; he holds a fly-whisk and a conch with his two right hands, and a discus and a mace with his two left hands.
Having formed the *añjali* mudrā with palms facing upward, one should bend the two index fingers and encircle them.
The conch mudrā; the mantra.
Oṃ āṃ śrī vajrapāṇaye svāhā.
Of Hari.
In the west is Brahmā, white in color, mounted upon a swan, with four faces. He holds a rosary and a parasol-staff in his right hands, and a lotus and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hands.
Interlocking the fingers one with another, one should extend only the little fingers;
this is the *kamaṇḍalu* mudrā. The mantra is: [mantra].
Oṃ, svāhā to the god, the teacher, the best of gods!
Of Brahmā.
To the north is Kārttikeya. He is red, adorned like a youth, has three heads, and stands upon a peacock. He holds a chowrie in his right hand and a spear (*śakti*) in his left.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the middle finger;
this is the *śakti-mudrā*. The mantra is: [mantra].
Oṃ hrīḥ, to the wielder of the spear against Krauñca, phaṭ!
Of the prince.

In the northeast is Gaṇapati, white, elephant-faced, mounted upon a mouse, with three eyes and bearing the crescent moon. With his two right hands he holds a radish and a battle-axe; with his two left hands he holds a trident and a skull-cup. Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the index and middle fingers; then, having contracted the index finger, one should form [the gesture] with the middle finger.
The Gaṇapati mudrā. The mantra:
Oṃ śrūṃ gaṇapataye svāhā.
Of Gaṇapati.
In the southeast is Ravi (the Sun). Mounted upon a horse-chariot, his body clad in armor, he is red in color and holds a lotus with his right and left hands.

Having formed the *añjali* gesture with palms facing upward, one should perform the *svastika* there. [Placing] the left little finger... [broken... having placed the right thumb... [broken... one should establish it.
The mudrā of Āditya. The mantra:
Oṃ śrī svaḥ sahasrakiraṇe svāhā.
Of the Sun.

In the southwest, Rāhu stands upon a chariot, red and black in color, with hair standing erect, and tawny eyebrows, beard, and mustache. His mouth is wide open, displaying four fangs, as he swallows the three worlds.
With his left eye, he forms the *añjali* gesture; extending his right hand, he should bend the index and ring fingers. This is the mudrā. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ, svāhā to the one whose prowess is equal to a hundred moons!
Of Rāhu.

In the north-western direction is Nāndikeśvara, yellow in color, performing a dance. He is consecrated by the crescent moon. A serpent serves as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). With his right and left hands, he holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a trident. [The Mudrā:

Pressing the little finger and ring finger of the right hand against the palm of the left hand, one forms a banner-like shape; likewise with the other hand. This same [gesture], when joined with the mantra, is the *samaya*-mudrā.
The mantra: Oṃ naṭeśvarāya naṭṭe 2 hrīḥ svāhā.
Of the Lord of the Dance (Narteśvara).
In the second enclosure:

to the north is Umā, yellow in color. She dances with her hands crossed above her head in the form of a serpent (*bhoga*), casting sidelong glances and displaying her eyes, armpits, and so forth. This very one, when joined with the mantra, is Samayā. The mantra is: [mantra].

Oṃ śrmyuṃ namaḥ. [This is] for Umā. To the east is Śrī, white in color; she holds a lotus flower at her heart with joined palms (añjali). That same gesture, when raised upward, is the Puṣpamudrā. The mantra is: [as above].
Oṃ Śrī Namaḥ.
Of the glories.

To the south is Tilottamā, red as a blue lotus, holding incense in her hand; she stands in a dancing posture, interposed between the others. She should place her joined palms (añjali) upon her head. This is the incense mudrā. The mantra is: [mantra].
Oṃ śi, homage!
Of Tilottamā.
In the west is Śaśī, red, holding a lamp.
Having formed a mutual fist and entwining the little fingers and index fingers, one should rotate them.
This is the lamp mudrā. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ śrī jaḥ namaḥ.
They are like the hare [mark].

In the southeast is Ratnaśrī, red in color, holding a scent-elephant. Forming a mutual fist with the two index fingers in the shape of a jewel, one should join them at the forehead in the manner of binding a garland.
This is the Gandha-mudrā. The mantra is: [mantra].
Oṃ Ratnaśrīḥ svāhā.
Of those adorned with jewels.
In the southwest is Sarasvatī, dark-green in color, playing a lute (*vīṇā*). She should place her two index fingers, having interlaced them with the other fingers, extended toward her mouth;
this is the *gīta-mudrā*. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ, to Sarasvatī, gādaya ṭha, all-svāhā!
Of Sarasvatī.
In the northwest is Yakṣeśvarī, black in color and wearing a red garland. Having formed a mutual fist, one should make the two little fingers into a ring;
this is the garland mudrā. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ yakṣeśvarī kṣī [kṣī] svāhā.
Of Surasundarī.

In the northeast is Ābhūtī, golden-colored, with dark blue, curled hair. She stands in the *narteśvara* (dancing lord) mudrā: having formed two fists with the hands facing each other, one should wrap the two little fingers around and curl the two index fingers. This is the Ābhūtī mudrā. The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ ābhūtī hrīḥ!
Of Ābhūti.

In the third enclosure, in the east, is Śakra, yellow in color, wearing a jewel crown, and mounted upon the white elephant Airāvata. In his left hand he holds his own weapon, the vajra; with the right he bestows fearlessness.
Extending the right hand, one should press the nail of the little finger with the thumb and spread the remaining fingers apart.
This is the Vajra-mudrā. The mantra is as follows: [mantra].
Oṃ, svāhā to Śakra!
Of Indra.

In the southeast is Agni. He is mounted on a goat, red in color, with three matted locks and a flaming beard. He has a protruding belly and three heads, wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and holds the gesture of boon-granting (*varada*) and a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in his two right hands. In his two left hands he carries a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). One should move the left hand, which forms the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), with the thumb slightly inserted. This is the mudrā of Agni. The mantra is: *Oṃ agnaye svāhā*. [This is for] Agni.

In the south is Yama. Seated upon a buffalo, he is red and black, pot-bellied, with tawny eyes and eyebrows, and a blazing tawny beard. [He has] matted hair... In his right hand he holds a staff marked with a skull; in his left [he holds] a noose. Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should extend the index finger—this is the *daṇḍamudrā*. The mantra is: Oṃ yamāya svāhā. [This is] for Yama.

In the southwest is a *rākṣasa* like Yama. This is his distinction: he is black, stands upon a *vetāḍa*, and holds a *dheṅga* (? in his right hand and [an object] in his left. Having formed a fist with the right hand and extending the index and middle fingers, this is the *dheṅga*-mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ rākṣasādhipataye jaya 2 svāhā*. [This is] for the *rākṣasa*.

In the west is Varuṇa, white in color, mounted upon a serpent with seven hoods. He holds a snake-noose in his left hand and displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in his right. Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should hold the index finger and thumb like a noose; this is the *pāśa-mudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ varuṇāya nāgādhipataye hasa 2 svāhā*. This is for Varuṇa.

In the northwest is Vāyu, blue in color, mounted upon a deer, a youth with three locks of hair. With his two arms he holds a garment of wind; having formed a fist with his left hand, he holds up his index finger like a noose. Extending his middle finger, he performs the banner mudrā. The mantra is: Oṃ vāyave cala 2 svāhā. [This is for] Vāyu.

In the north is Kuvera, mounted on a bull, yellow in color, stout, pot-bellied, and wearing a jeweled crown. He holds a mace and a mongoose in his left hands. Forming a fist with the right hand and extending the thumb constitutes the *gadā-mudrā* (mace gesture). The mantra is: *oṃ kuverāya yakṣādhipataye svāhā*. This is for Kuvera. In the northeast is Candra, mounted on a swan, bestowing boons with his right hand, and wearing garments made of moonlight. Forming a fist with both hands and joining the two little fingers together constitutes the *candra-mudrā* (moon gesture). The mantra is: *oṃ candrāya svāhā*.
And having bound Īśāna there, just as Maheśvara was [bound], with the Indravajra-mudrā, the root-mudrā-mantra of that very one is: Oṃ īśānāya svāhā. This is for Īśāna.

However, it should be understood that those mudrās such as the vajra which have been taught for these [worldly deities] are to be known as facing downward and marked with tridents and vajras; whereas, for the supramundane [deities], the vajra and other mudrās, on the contrary, face upward. || o ||
On the fourth layer.

To the east is Śuklasiṃhadhvajabhūtasiṃhadhvajādhārī. Forming a mutual fist, one should encircle the two index fingers; this is the Siṃhadhvaja-mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ bhūḥ śrīsiṃhadhvajadhāriṇī hrīḥ*. [This is] for Siṃhadhvajadhāriṇī. To the south is Vibhūti. She is red and holds a goad (*aṅkuśa*). Forming a fist with the right hand, one should extend the index finger and bend it; this is the Aṅkuśa-mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ śrīvibhūti aṅkuśadhāriṇī hūṃ jaḥ*. [This is] for Vibhūti.

In the west is Mahāpadmavajradhanurbāṇadhāriṇī, who is white. Having formed a mutual fist and extended the index fingers, she places them at the region of her left hip; this is the mudrā of the bow and arrow. The mantra is: Oṃ hūṃ bhū mahāpadmavatī dhanurbāṇadhāriṇī hūṃ. [This is] for Mahāpadmavatī.

To the north is Surahāriṇī, red in color, holding a wish-fulfilling jewel banner (*cintāmaṇidhvaja*). Having formed a fist with the left hand and extending the middle finger, this is the *cintāmaṇidhvaja* mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ bhu hūṃ bhūḥ surahāriṇī cintāmaṇidhvajadhāriṇī srūṃ*. [This is] for Surahāriṇī.

In the northeast is Varahāriṇī, yellow in color. [Her mudrā is] at the heart: having formed an *añjali* with palms facing upward, the two index fingers are bent; this is the Varahāriṇī mudrā. With this very [mudrā], the mantra for the flower-offering is: *oṃ śrīdharahāriṇī puṣpahaste hūṃ śrīḥ*. This is for Varahāriṇī.

In the southeast is Mahāratneśvarī, yellow in color, holding incense in her hand. She entwines her fingers with one another and extends both index fingers. This is the incense mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ ratneśvarī dhūpahaste hūṃ*. [This is] for Ratneśvarī. In the southwest is Bhūṣaṇī, golden in appearance, holding a perfumed conch in her hand. She extends her hands toward one another and places them at the base of her arms. This is the perfume mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ śrībhūṣaṇī gandhahaste hūṃ*. [This is] for Śrībhūṣaṇī.

In the northwest is Jagatpālanī, yellow in color, holding a lamp-stick in her hand. Having made a fist with her right hand and pointing its fingers downward, she extends one finger; this is the lamp mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ śrījagatpālanī dīpahaste aḥ*. [This is] for Jagatpālanī.

All these deities are seated upon their respective thrones in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, adorned with various ornaments and garments. They possess various radiant halos and are embellished with all types of decorations.

Then, having placed the seed-syllable upon the five-pronged vajra in the moon of one’s own heart, the pledge-mudrās (samayamudrā) should be applied as before. One should place the respective mantra on their tongues. [The] mudrā: by means of the meditation on the universal vajra (viśvavajra) in the heart, there is the mudrā arising from that which is devoid of signs. The great mudrā (mahāmudrā) arises from the mastery of the essence. Then, having drawn Mahādeva and the others into the bodies of Mahādeva and the others by means of the mantra of the summoning mudrā, and having caused them to enter, one should establish them in the pledge (samaya). Brandishing the vajra: "This vajra is the Great Vajra, empowered by all the Buddhas."
"By transgressing the samaya, he will swiftly reduce your families to ashes," saying:
*oṃ hana samaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then: *oṃ vajraratna trāṃ*.

Thus, in the vajra-binding, with the thumbs and index fingers joined at the shoulders and the middle fingers bent, one should consecrate all the deities with this [mudrā], gaze with a lion’s look, and speak thus:
"O Great King, accomplished in wrath, accomplish the teaching of the pledge!
May all the deities swiftly attain supreme accomplishment!"
Awakened by this, they all became afraid and stood facing their own respective accomplishments.

Then, one should worship Umā and the others, together with the obstacles, as well as the Blessed One Mahādeva and the rest. Oṃ! O Umā, at the time of the radiation of the cloud of worship for the protection of passion, worship the Great Vajra-Wrath; homage!
Oṃ [omitted syllables] pūjāmeghaspharaṇasamaye pūjaya mahāvajrakrodhaṃ svāhā.

Oṃ! Sarasvatī, with lute in hand, cause [the sound] to resound! At the time of the manifestation of the cloud of worship consisting of all songs, perform worship to the Great Vajra Wrathful One, svāhā!
Oṃ! O you who possess the hand of manifestation, at the time of the radiation of clouds of dance-offerings, worship the Great Wrathful One!
Oṃ [8] O you who hold a flower in your hand, at the time of the radiation of the cloud of offerings, worship the glorious Great Vajra Wrath! Oṃ Śrī Namaḥ!
Oṃ Tilottame, you who hold incense in your hand, at the time of the radiation of the cloud of incense offerings, worship the glorious Great Vajra Wrath! Jaḥ!
Oṃ śrī jaḥ! O Śaśidevī, with lamp in hand, at this time of the radiation of clouds of lamp-offerings, worship the Great Vajra Wrath; homage!
Oṃ, to Ratnaśrī, O you who hold a fragrant hand, at the time of the pervasive cloud of fragrance-offerings, worship the Great Vajra Wrath; svāhā!
Then follows the mantra for the worship of the gatekeepers and others.
Oṃ! O bearer of the glorious lion-banner, reveal the great vajra-wrath of the Lion-Banner; satisfy him! Hrīḥ!
Oṃ, O Vibhūti, wielder of the goad, summon the Great Vajra Wrath; bring him under control! Hūṃ Jaḥ!
Oṃ hūṃ bhūḥ! O Mahāpadmavatī, bearer of bow and arrow, arouse the great Vajra-wrath! Hūṃ!
Oṃ hūṃ bhūḥ! O you who seize the gods, bearer of the wish-fulfilling jewel banner, reveal the great vajra wrath, the wish-fulfilling jewel-treasure banner! Śruṃ!
Oṃ, you who take away [obstacles], with flowers in hand, at the time of the radiation of clouds of flower-offerings, worship the Great Vajra Wrath, hūṃ!
Oṃ Ratneśvarī! You who hold incense in your hand, at this time of the emanation of clouds of incense offerings, worship the Vajra Great Wrathful One! Hūṃ!
Oṃ! Śrī Jagatpālanī, you who hold a lamp in your hand; at this time of the radiating cloud of lamp-offerings, worship the Great Wrathful One: Aḥ!
Oṃ vibhūṣaṇi gandhahaste, at the time of the pervasion of clouds of fragrance-offerings, worship the Great Wrathful One! Hūṃ śrīṃ!

Then, having emanated the seven precious jewels, food of the six flavors, and so forth by means of the syllable *oṃ*, one should offer them. Then, standing in the center of the maṇḍala and possessing the yoga of one’s own tutelary deity,
one should meditate upon oneself as the agent of emanation and reabsorption.

When weariness arises, one should take up the Wrath-Vajra with the left wrathful fist, while holding the rosary at the heart with the other hand—the ring finger and thumb—and recite the name one hundred and eight times, one thousand and eight times, or more, using either the speech of the Wrathful One or the speech of Vajra.

While meditating on the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) within the heart, one should visualize the syllables of the mantra appearing in his heart; from that, rays of light emerge from body, speech, and mind. Having exhorted [the deity] together with his family, and having grasped and returned, they enter the Leader all at once. Visualizing in this manner, one should perform the recitation. Thus it is said.
In this way, all the deities of the maṇḍala are to be visualized as uttering the mantra.
Now, the speech of the wrathful ones is like a swirling cloud, profound with the sound of *hūṃ*; it is the firm vajra-speech.
One who is intensely wrathful with great fury is accomplished as Vajravāg.
Then, Vajravāg does not leak [semen], her tongue-tip joined with both lips and teeth.
"Applicable to all kalpas, vajra-speech is devoid of vocal sound.
In this regard, the meaning of recitation (*jāpa*) is as follows:
The teaching cuts through the bonds of suffering and existence;
it terrifies and slays the wicked. The syllable *hūṃ* is the stage of slaying;
it is the total abandonment of conceptual construction and the relinquishing of all grasping at phenomena.

The suchness of all phenomena is emptiness, which is known as the vajra. It is known as the casting down of all the wicked, the bliss, and the summoning. One who is incapable of casting down through the syllable *haṃ* destroys rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*).

Thus spoke the Blessed Lord, the Vajra-holder. Having performed this yoga at the morning twilight (*pūrvasandhyā*), the entire yoga should not be performed again at the subsequent twilight. Rather, having brought [the deity] forth by means of the mudrā and mantra, and having performed worship, praise, and the offering of the three pledges (*trisamaya*), one should perform meditation or recitation (*japa*). One should accomplish [the practice] during the intervals between twilights through the yoga of ease (*yathāsukhayoga*). Taking recourse in equality with space and through the yoga of unifying with all deities, one should practice while walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping; this is the yoga of ease.
When the empowerment of the mudrā becomes slackened, or when one wishes to speak oneself, then one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra.

Having thus performed the meditation or the recitation, if one becomes weary, one should first offer praise with the "Hundred Names," perform worship as before, and likewise offer the water for the guest (argha) and the water for the feet (pādya), saying this:

Having formed the *saṃpuṭāñjali* mudrā for the sake of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure and for the accomplishment of success within oneself, [one recites]: *oṃ siddhivajra āpūraya 2 hūṃ*.

Then, one should revive the great being Aparājita as before. Having visualized him arisen, one should worship him with the fourfold worship beginning with Umā. Having worshipped him, one should ask for his forgiveness.
Then, one should urge the Blessed One, together with his assembly and retinue, to depart, using this mudrā-mantra:
having formed the lotus-seat mudrā (*padmāsana-mudrā*), one should raise the left thumb.
Oṃ, go, go! Śrīvajradhara commands: svāhā hūṃ muḥ!
Thus they are dismissed. O.
