[1] Having thus performed the preliminary service, one should draw the maṇḍala every day, every month, or every year according to this procedure.

Equipped with all necessary implements, on a chosen plot of ground, one should ward off obstacles by performing an *abhicāruka* oblation of powdered human bone; then, having performed a pacifying (*śāntika*) oblation for the sake of oneself and one's disciple, and having expelled the malevolent spirits with the mantra for the expulsion of the wicked, one should protect the site as before by means of the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) and other rites. Then, having dug the earth to a depth of knee-, waist-, or navel-height according to the distinction between inferior, middling, or superior accomplishments, and having removed hair and other debris, one should fill it with pure, fragrant, and well-anointed clay.

Having sprinkled [the ground] with scented water consecrated by mantras for the expulsion of evil spirits, and having leveled it, one should prepare the site of the mandala within a peaked pavilion, enclosed by four gateways and a fence, starting from the eastern direction, smeared with fragrant substances and glowing [with colors], and containing a ball of five jewels, medicinal herbs, and grains hidden in the center.

However, on a paved floor or similar surface, one should scatter mustard seeds, water, and ashes—each recited seven times—for the expulsion of obstacles and the binding of the directions; then, having smeared it as before and sprinkled it with scented water, one should place the jewels and other items in the center. This is the procedure for purifying the ground.
Then, having fully worshipped the Earth Goddess, who arises from the syllable *vaṃ* and holds a treasure-trove in her hand:
"O Goddess, you are the witness for all the Buddhas, the Protectors,
regarding the specificities of the conduct and methods, and the stages and perfections."
"Just as the army of Māra was shattered by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas, so too, having achieved victory over Māra, I shall draw the maṇḍala.

Having thus exhorted [the deities] with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Akṣobhya and worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, one should contemplate the offerings (bali) right there. Then, having placed the hand upon the ground which is duly adorned with flowers and other items, one should repeat the syllable *HŪṂ* and the four-syllable mantra twenty-one times. This is the ritual appropriation of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*).

Then, standing in the center of the mandala ground, having performed the yoga-posture and other preliminaries as before, and seated upon the central throne, one should gladden oneself [with these words]:
"Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life too is fruitful;
I shall undoubtedly become equal to the deities of the pledge (*samaya*)."
I shall become irreversible, with a single-minded intent toward enlightenment;
today my birth in the great Vajra family shall occur, of this there is no doubt.
For today is indeed my foremost day, and today my sacrifice is unsurpassed.
"Today indeed is my supreme assembly, because of the invitation to all the Buddhas. Then, with incense sticks in hand, one should invite them by bowing with all one's limbs to all the Buddhas.
May the Protectors dwelling in all directions without exception attend to me:
I, the Vajra-holder named [Name], am preparing the maṇḍala.

Having said, "May all the Buddhas and others come; you shall grant this accomplishment," one should stand in the center of the maṇḍala as before, meditate on oneself as Mahāvajradhara performing the emanation and reabsorption [of light], and while reciting the mantra with wrathful speech, one should manifest the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).

Then, for the purpose of drawing the maṇḍala, the Wrathful Lord is to be requested by the assistant practitioners—who have assumed the forms of Mahādeva and others—after they have circumambulated him three times to the right and performed prostrations at his feet.

May the Great Bodhisattva speak the secret mandala of all accomplishments, which possesses unimpeded command, is honored by the three realms, is a great king who strikes fear into all bhūtas, nāgas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas, is the destroyer of all obstacles and impediments, the eradicator of suffering and afflictions, and the slayer of all grahas, vetālas, kaṭapūtanas, and māras.
Then, having emerged and seen the sky filled with all the Tathāgatas, he prostrated at their feet.
I myself am the Vajra-holder; I myself am Vajrasattva.
I am the Buddha, the Great King; I am the Vajra-holder of great power.
I am the King, the Lord of Yogins; I am the firm Vajrapāṇi.
I am the Lord Mahāvajra; I do not abandon my empowerment.

Then, the Vajrācārya who has obtained the three samayas, holding the vajra and bell with his own mudrā, should perform all the ritual procedures of the maṇḍala-cakra. Having manifested the maṇḍala according to the rules by means of the mudrā of the Blessed One, he should raise it up with the mantra "HŪṂ VAJROTTHA" (O Vajra, Arise!

and establish the maṇḍala in space. Then, having empowered himself with his own mantra, he should adopt a wrathful gaze. Placing "HĪḤ" upon his eyes, with his brow deeply furrowed, his eyes contracted with a frowning expression of rage.
Rising in that very manner, standing in the mudrā and looking in all directions, he should circumambulate with self-pride while reciting his own mantra.

With the soles of his feet empowered by the universal vajra arising from the final vowel, he makes the surface of the earth into a blazing vajra. Having performed the expulsion of obstacles and the binding of the directions as before, he constructs a fence and a cage with the vajra-gaze.
The union with Śrī Vajrasattva is characterized by the clenching together of the upper and lower lips.
The glorious one, whose lower lip is slightly curved to the left, clearly performs the gesture of the circle of directions.
Then, having presided over the upper [space], one should bind *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
Uttering the syllable *hūṃ*, which is difficult for the evil-minded to enter.

Then, with the mantra *oṃ vajramaṇḍala hūṃ jaḥ* and the mudrā of the double-vajra fist with the thumbs extended at the tips, one draws forth the secret maṇḍala— four-faced, four-armed, and possessing the power of the vajra cause—
with the mantra *oṃ vajracakre ’dhiṣṭhita siddhya hūṃ*.
One should consecrate [the site] with the mudrā of the whirling firebrand of the two vajras.

Then, having consecrated with mantra the stakes (*kila*) made of *khadira* wood—namely, those called Ananta-vijaya, Meghanāda, Mahodara, and Jaya, which are respectively the forms of Trilokavijaya, Yamāri, Mahābala, and Hayagrīva, and which are shaped like tridents at their bases—one should smear them with red sandalwood paste, bind them with red thread, and adorn them with red garlands. Taking them with the left fist, one should drive them into the four corners of the outer maṇḍala starting from the northeast with the "Vajra-Truth" mantra:
*oṃ vajrakīla kīlaya sarvavighnān bandha 2 hūṃ phaṭ*.

And having performed, in sequence, the binding of the protective armor with the vajra-yakṣa-rakṣa fists upon those [parts], one should place the water jar at the door of the maṇḍala house with the mantra for the expulsion of the wicked.

Having sprinkled [the area] and smeared the ground of the maṇḍala with fragrant water over which that [mantra] has been recited, at all the locations of the deities within the fragrant maṇḍala where their names have been invoked, one should visualize the deities of the maṇḍala descending from the sky; having established them within one’s own heart, worshipped them, and invoked them, one should offer the *bali* oblation. [The vessel] should be made of the seven precious gems or of clay, shaped like a jar with a root at the bottom, a hanging lip, a long neck, and a broad belly, bound with a well-woven cloth, its mouth adorned with sprouts and leaves, and marked with the insignia of one’s own deity.

Regarding the victory vase (*vijayakalaśa*): it should be filled with coral, gold, conch, pearl-oyster, and ruby gems; with *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭhakārī*, *sahī*, *daṇḍotpala*, white *aparājitā*, and *ugragandhā*; and with rice, barley, wheat, beans, sesame, and *vrīhi* grains. Having recited the Blessed One’s mantra over it one hundred and eight times, having added a small amount of fragrant water for the offering (*argha*), and having duly generated the Blessed One there by means of the syllable *HŪṂ* and performed worship, one should take a flower garland with the mudrā for dispelling obstacles, recite that mantra one hundred and eight times, scatter loose flowers, and offer incense.

Having performed everything in this manner even with the four-syllable [mantra], incense should be offered. Likewise on the day of the mandala; one should consecrate [the objects] with these two at the three junctions of the day. Then, one should place them before the Blessed One. This is the ritual procedure for the consecration of the vases. || O ||

Then, having invoked Śakra and the others according to the previously mentioned procedure, having displayed their respective mudrās and mantras, having offered water for sipping (ācamana), having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having presented the bali offering, one should dismiss the Nāga with the mantra: *oṃ śara 2 gaccha gaccha*, etc. Above, [there are] Candra, Ārka, and Brahmā; one should direct the gaze upward. Below, [the mantra is]: *amurebhyaḥ svāhā* || *nāgebhyaḥ svāhā* || The bali should be given with the vajra-joined palms (vajrāñjali) extended.

There is another method: having offered red food, flowers, incense, and so forth, one should cover the *bali* offering with a white cloth and invoke the deity with this [mantra]: "O great being born of the divine, having prostrated, I dismiss you. Just as the great being, may you release the place of wrath—*svāhā*. Then, having consecrated it with this [mantra], one should present it to them; having prostrated, one should present it, saying: "O great being born of the divine."

"Go each to your respective abodes among the great elements; go there to the cremation grounds, the temples of the gods, solitary trees, riverbanks, crossroads, solitary lingas, and divine shrines. Let the spirits go quickly to observe their covenant. If they do not go, he shall split their heads with the vajra; in an instant he shall destroy them, and they shall fall into the Raurava hell. ...
[The disciples], with flowers in their hands, should bow to the teacher and speak thus:

"You are my teacher, O Great Hero! I desire, O Great Protector, the firm method of the Bodhisattvas; grant me the commitment (*samaya*), grant me the reality (*tattva*), and grant me the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)."
"Grant me the three refuges: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha! O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.

Then, facing the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, [the master] visualizes the *samaya* syllable *aḥ* in the hearts of the disciples; by means of this, he emanates a moon disc, and upon that, a vajra by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. With his right hand in the vajra-fist gesture...
Having placed the vajra at his heart with [the mantra] *hṛdayena*,

the master should say, "O Vajra, you are the pledge (*samaya*) in the state of great bliss; accomplish [it], O Hero, according to your pleasure," and then cause him to perform the confession of sins and so forth.
I pay homage to all the Sugatas together with their Dharma and great assemblies—
to those leaders who know nothing unknown and who always protect the world; to them alone I go for refuge with my whole being.
I have wandered through the world in suffering, yet I am not afflicted by those sufferings.
Resolved to propitiate them in every way and at all times, I offer myself to them; may the Leaders accept me!
I confess every sin and shall not commit it again.
I rejoice in all that is virtuous, whether performed by myself or by others.
May the perfectly awakened Buddhas teach the Dharma; may they never pass into parinirvāṇa. May sentient beings be made happy and may they proceed to the supreme state.
And having become omniscient and established in the state of all sovereignty,
may I deliver the entire world from the ocean of existence on every side.
And for the sake of attaining Buddhahood, I shall persevere according to my strength;
I make this firm vow, remaining unattached therein.
Likewise, in all my births, may I exert myself in the means for that [liberation]; may I be a master of all prosperity, faultless, virtuous, and happy;
and whatever merit has been performed by me, and whatever I shall perform—[may it all be for that end].
"By this, may the state of a Sugata be accomplished for me and for this world.

Then, Ratnaśrī should place incense in [the disciple's] hand; Śrī, flowers; Tilottamā, incense; and Śaśī, a lamp. With the mantra "Vajrahāsa," one should take a tooth-stick made of *udumbara* or *aśvattha* wood, wrapped with flowers and scented with perfume, and after chewing its tip, it should be thrown directly forward.

Having given the scented water consecrated with the *vajradharma* mantra for sipping, he should say: "Oṃ hrīḥ, O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person and remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ vajratīkṣṇa! Having recited this, he should place one fresh blade of *kuśa* grass on the head and give the others, consecrated with the *vajrarakṣa* mantra, for spreading as a seat. Then, having himself tied a large thread with three knots on his left arm using the *vajrakavaca* mantra, he should protect [the disciple] with the mantras and mudrās of the six limbs and speak the Dharma.
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains,
in that you have all been accepted here into this teaching by all the Victors together with their Sons, as they were being born as great-souled beings.
By this you shall indeed be well-born in the Mahāyāna;
this is the glorious, supreme path, the great exaltation of the Mahāyāna, by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas.
The self-existent ones are highly fortunate, the physicians for all the worlds.
It transcends existence and non-existence, stainless like space;
it is profound, beyond all ratiocination, inconceivable, and without abode.
It is devoid of all conceptual proliferation, yet it is manifested through conceptual proliferations.
Free from ritual action and the like, and resting upon the two truths— this supreme and most excellent vehicle you shall attain by abiding in this method.

"Thus, arise, O gentle-faced ones! Tomorrow, through the grace of the Great Vajradhara, you shall behold the city of Great Liberation. Having spoken thus, he should offer incense and invite the Blessed One together with his retinue, saying:
"O Blessed One, [Name] King of Vidyās, homage be to you!"
Tomorrow, being compassionate by nature, I wish to draw the mandala out of compassion for my disciples and for your worship.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to show favor to me, your devotee.
I, named so-and-so, [enter] the auspicious mandala called so-and-so.
When tomorrow has dawned, I shall write it out for you according to my ability and with proper ritual service;
this is my duty toward you, my excellent disciple, out of compassion.
One should say three times: "May you all, together in the maṇḍala, deign to be present.

Then, having worshipped and offered the *argha* to the maṇḍala, the master—along with the disciples, having performed his ablutions, being free from debt, and having established the yoga of the deity—should likewise project the maṇ᾽ala into the space above. [He should do so] with five colored threads dyed with fragrant substances that are white, yellow, red, green, and blue, mixed with the powder of *sihlātaka*.

Having established [the deities] in this very sequence, one should visualize Vairocana and the other Sugatas as *Āḥ Trāṃ Hrīḥ Aḥ Hūṃ*. Having meditated that threads of light from their own seed-syllables are dispatched from their respective hearts by these [deities] stationed in their own directions, [one recites]:
*Oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyāṅkuśī jaḥ*.

Having thus placed [the mantra] upon his own eye, with eyes moving rapidly and flickering, and having drawn the external thread held in his hand by means of the hook of his blazing gaze—his eyes fixed on the drawing of the eyelashes—he should fill it three times and coil it while reciting:
"All phenomena follow one another; all phenomena have entered into one another; all phenomena have entered into one another completely, hūṃ!"

Then, having placed [the thread] in a golden vessel or similar container filled with fragrant powder, having worshipped it, and having secured it with the vajra-bind, the Lord of the Maṇḍala consecrates it one hundred and eight times with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasamayasūtra mātikrama hūṃ*. Having thus adorned the ground of the maṇḍala, he remains stationed in the intermediate space. Having worshipped the maṇḍala with flowers and other offerings, his eyes become yellowish-white moon and sun produced by two *jaḥ* syllables; then, having emanated the northern practitioner in the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalin with the syllable *hūṃ*, and taking the thread with his left vajra-fist, he should hold it at his navel.

Having issued the command "Oṃ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ," the assistant practitioner likewise draws [the thread] with "Oṃ ja ja ja" and stands facing him in the same manner. The Vajra-holder, positioned toward the east and north, situated in the directions of the Lord of Nagas and the Lord of Pretas, stretches two sky-threads and, having determined the equality of all directions, likewise casts two axle-threads upon the ground. This thread should be drawn with a thickness of one-twentieth of the door and a length twice that of the maṇḍala, using the previous vajra-mudrā.
One should subsequently hold the thread; this is known as the proper method of threading.

Facing the directions of the Yakṣas, Pretas, Devas, Nāgas, and so forth, and remaining in the directions of Fire (South-East) and Wind (North-West), one should lay out four threads for the Guru—east, west, north, and south—thereby forming a fourfold grid. One should also [lay out] eight mandalas. In this very sequence, one should thread the lines.

By the sound of the laying of the threads, one should visualize that the Tathāgatas, pervading the sky, are exhorted and arrive here at the time for the benefit of sentient beings, thinking: "O you who act for the sake of beings, come here!"
And in all cases, one should circumambulate the Guru and the senior practitioner from the right.
[5] Again, standing in the southeast, and having stood in the northwest and southwest, one should extend the cord as far as the northeast corner.
It is square, with four gates and endowed with four archways;
it is furnished with sixteen sections and adorned with a vajra-rampart.

This is what is meant: one should construct a square measuring one-fourth of the outer mandala, joined with eight compartments (*koṣṭhaka*), with an inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*) surrounded on the outside by a garland of vajras (*vajrāvalī*). One should make three enclosures (*puṭa*) on each of the two sides. In every case, in the middle portion, the doors (*dvāra*) shall consist of eight parts; the door-projections (*niryūha*), pilasters (*kapola*), and side-wings (*pakṣaka*) shall be half the measure of the doors. Outside the main line (*mūlasūtra*), the ground for colored powder (*rajobhūmi*) shall be half the measure of the pilasters. Outside of that, the altars (*vedikā*) shall be equal in measure to the pilasters.

The dimensions of the outer dust-line (rajobhūmi) are equal to those of the necklaces, half-necklaces, and fillets; the ground for the lines of the eight pillars, beginning with the vajra, is equal to the dust-line. The archway (toraṇa) above the door is three times the width of the door. Thus it is for both the outer and inner enclosures, according to the proportions of the mandala; at the corners of the wheel (cakra), there should be banners, bells, chowries, wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), and so forth.

Then, having driven a ritual stake (kīlaka) into the center of the mandala as before, shaped like a five-pronged vajra, one should [fix] the cord for the qualities (guṇasūtra) shaped like two vajras attached to it. One should then lay out the outer vajra-line and the circle of light (prabhāmaṇḍala) from the inner and outer mandalas respectively.
If anyone were unfit for the casting of the thread,
then he himself should cast it by tying it to a stake, even without an assistant.

Others [say]: "The inner [mandala] is circular, surrounded by a garland of vajras; the second has one line, the third has three lines, and the fourth is five-colored; the third [mandala] is square with three enclosures. In this regard, having divided sixteen parts by means of seventeen lines, there is a circular [area] consisting of eight squares, surrounded by a garland of vajras.

They sever everything previously bound; then, having established the moon and sun in the left and right eyes by means of the syllable *Hrīḥ* alone, and having looked with a wrathful gaze and secured the doors, one should thus lay out the lines and then release the wisdom-line (*jñānasūtra*).

Then, from the seed-syllables *vaṃ*, *laṃ*, *raṃ*, *haṃ*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*, one should produce in sequence the auspicious [colored powders] as described in the Sūtra—white and so forth—in order of their colors: those born of jewels, those arising from the five metals, or those produced from minerals; or else, those made from parched rice, from baked bricks, or from black charcoal. These [powders] are produced by means of the syllables *āḥ*, *trāṃ*, *hrīḥ*, *aḥ*, and *hūṃ*, and consist of the nature of the family-mudrās (*kulamudrā*). Then, with the mantra *oṃ vajracitta sama hūṃ*, one should perform the vajra-mudrā for the pair [of deities], which is endowed with the supreme equality.
Having performed [this] for all the ritual components (*raṅga*), one should summon [them] with a blazing gaze.

Having caused that [object] to enter and having transformed it into the form of its ultimate atoms, one should intensify it with the syllable *hrīḥ*. Then, having meditated upon the wrathful Vajrasūrya with the syllable *oṃ*, one should set it ablaze with the mantra and mudrā of that [deity], saying "hūṃ phaṭ" while holding the two vajra-fists at the heart amidst garlands of solar flames.
Then, having uprooted the stake (*kīlaka*) situated at the navel of the maṇḍala with the syllable *hūṃ*—

Having inserted the vajra held in his own hand into the pit of the kīla and filled it with five-colored powders, he should dispel ill omens through the sounding of the bell, vajra-songs, and so forth, [reciting]:
"This is the pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the liberator of the realm of sentient beings;
the King, Vajradhara himself, shall now begin the casting of the colored powders."

At the very beginning, with the left fist, standing within and starting from the northeastern direction (aiśānī), one should cast [the lines]. Afterwards, as is convenient: continuous, without gaps, unbroken, and proceeding clockwise. In the sequence of white, yellow, red, green, and blue; in the second enclosure (puṭa), the three colors are white, red, and black; in the two inner enclosures, by black alone. Each color [should be] for the thickness of twenty parts of the line and door? [The measurement? ... on the ground? The eastern [direction] is yellow, the western red, the northern green, and the middle black.

If an obstacle should arise while the mandala is being drawn, then one should dispel it by means of the prescribed ritual, using the mudrā and mantra for the removal of obstacles, or through the cultivation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Then, in the center: *jā* *naṃ* *hrīḥ*. *Oṃ* [etc. *sūryākrāntām* (surmounted by the sun). For the others, a lotus.

Then, in the center, one should cause the Blessed One—who possesses the previously described color and form—to arrive from the sky as a single entity while reciting his own mantra along with *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, or else one should cause him to enter by means of the *samayamudrā* while uttering *hūṃ*. In this manner, while reciting *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, one should cause Maheśvara and the others—distinguished by their respective faces, arms, and colors as previously described—to enter their appropriate positions facing the Blessed One, using each one’s own *samayamudrā* and mantra. In all cases, during the entry into and exit from the maṇḍala, one should recite *vajra hūṃ*. This is the procedure for the mudrās.
If one mentally crosses over a line, or even a line of Vajrasūrya,
or a line for the Buddha’s discarded offerings (nirmālya), one incurs fault whether done intentionally or unintentionally.

Then, as before, the area outside the maṇḍala should be smeared all around with fragrant water; one should offer a profusion of flowers and incense burners—eight or five—in an uninterrupted stream. Having performed the sprinkling ritual seven times as before, then at the time of afternoon, possessing the pride of the Wrathful One and uttering the four-syllable mantra, having bound the pledge (samaya), and taking blue flowers, one enters the maṇḍala, rings the bell, and circumambulates it three times.
O! Having thus taken up the Blessed Lady through the yoga of one's own nature, and having bound her to one's own head with the syllable *hūṃ*, one stands in the center of the maṇḍala;
firmly joining the two vajra-fingers with their palms facing upward.
Oṃ, open the vajra; enter the pledge, hūṃ!
Being well-angered, standing in the western direction, one should mentally open the doors—those of the east and so forth—by means of the *alīḍha* stance and other such postures.

Then, as previously described: the flask, smeared with external perfume and empowered by the blazing vajra, is recited over as before: Oṃ tiṣṭha siddhi hūṃ. Having bound the pledge (*samaya*) with this, it is taken up with the *kuyamalatā* [mudrā].

Having recited the four-syllable mantra eight thousand times, and likewise having taken [the water] that has been recited over, one should circumambulate the outer and inner mandalas three times, place it before the Lord, and set down another flask—recited over one hundred and eight times with the four-syllable mantra—facing the entrance door. Having sprinkled oneself and the disciples with that water, and having bound the *pāśikī* wrathful mudrā, [one should invoke] the flasks of Maheśvara and the others with their own respective mantras.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should place it outside the nine-fold mandala. Outside [that], there should be full jars (*pūrṇakumbha*). In their absence, one should use the victory-vessels (*vijaya-kalaśa*) for the self-sprinkling; one jar each for Maheśvara, Śakra, Āditya, and others—namely Śrīpadmavatī, Ratnaśrī, and Mahāratnavatī. Following this very sequence, one should cause the remaining [deities] to be worshipped on the tenth day. And one should offer ten full jars.

[6] Then, having meditated upon the maṇḍala situated there and made a request: "Oṃ, with prostration to the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, I perform the vajra-salutation. Having prostrated and taken up the going for refuge and so forth as before, one should take the vow:
"I generate the supreme, unsurpassed bodhicitta, just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment."
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of wholesome qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall uphold the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha with respect to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the unsurpassed, supreme Triple Gem.
I shall truly receive the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā.
I shall accept a master in the exalted Mahāvajra family;
I shall bestow the four gifts six times every day,
within the worthy Mahāratna family, at the delightful and auspicious time.
I accept the True Dharma— outer and secret, belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which originates from Great Awakening.
I accept, in accordance with reality, the vow that is fully integrated with all [these].
One should perform the rite of worship according to one's ability within the exalted assembly of the Mahākarma family.
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed bodhicitta;
I have undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings.
"I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are unliberated;
I shall give rest to those who are weary, and I shall establish them in nirvāṇa.

Then, having uttered [this], he—wearing blue garments, with a turban on his head, adorned with garlands, his face fragrant, and decorated with all ornaments—stands outside, his face veiled in blue cloth as recited by the female gatekeepers. Having consecrated him with water from the jar and armored him with the wrathful [mantra], one should say this:
Bestowing accomplishment at that very moment for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, O Great Wrathful One, Accomplished Vajra, abide, O deity of the pledge!

Then, having bound the wrathful mudrā and uttering "Vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ," one enters by means of the Vajrakrodhā [deity] to be described. Having caused oneself to be possessed, one abides [with the thought] "O Vajra... and so forth, [placing the deity] in the heart. [Then follows] the consecration with the garland-throwing of the jar-garland at that very moment.

Having performed the unveiling of the face and the display of the wheel, one should visualize everything—from the water and other consecrations up to the bestowal of the three pledges—as being performed by the preceptor who has entered existence, just as before.

Then, having received the permission through the offering of the song of the three pledges, the five verses of praise, the four-syllable mantra, and the prophecy of the *udgatā* verse, one should re-enter, perform the rites up to the taking of the vajra-vow, utter one's own name saying "I am [Name]vajra," and accomplish the mandala.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: having bound the mudrā of the Blessed One with its mantra ending in the final vowel; then, having established oneself in the place as Krodhavajra and formed the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) "I am Krodhavajra"; and having visualized [oneself] as Vajra Mahācakradhara and formed the ego-identification "I am the Lord of Wrath."

Having invoked the Blessed One together with the deities of the maṇḍala by means of the previously mentioned *āvāhana-mudrā*, and having praised him with hymns beginning with "O Primordial One," one should, as before, perform the expulsion of evil beings, the binding of the directions, and the construction of the enclosure and cage; then, having offered the *argha* and *pādya* waters, one should accomplish the practice at the end [of the recitation] with the words "Samaya tvam" preceded by the *samaya* syllables: *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

Having thus meditated upon the wheel of deities (devatācakra), which consists of the mantras for protecting the world beginning with Mahādeva and is endowed with their respective insignia, and having completed the process up to the accomplishment, sealing, and consecration, one should perform worship with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra for expelling the wicked. Having sprinkled [the site] and offered the water of honor (argha), one should mark each [deity] with two insignia or a single one for all of them. Then, having recited the syllable *oṃ* over various kinds of canopies, banners, parasols, and flags, one should effect the expansion of the wheel (*cakrasphāraṇa*) and dedicate [the offering] with this [mantra].

Then, having consecrated the perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps with the ocean-like *vajrānala* mantra: "Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ," one offers the perfumes according to what is available by means of the perfume mudrā; likewise, "Oṃ vajrapuṣpe aṃ" for the flowers by means of the flower mudrā; "Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ" for the incenses by means of the incense mudrā; and "Oṃ vajrāloke hūṃ" for the lamps by means of the lamp mudrā.

Having recited the mantra *vajraspharaṇa khaṃ* and offered [the oblation], one should likewise offer various kinds of foods—solid, soft, lickable, suckable, and drinkable—with the *svastika* and other gestures. With the mantra *oṃ ākāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt* and the mudrā of brandishing a sword (*khaḍgotkarṣaṇābhinayamudrā*) for the offering of fragrant substances (*vajragandha*), one should perform the gesture of playing musical instruments with the fingers of both vajra-fists. And with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should play the music.

[Reciting] *oṃ ka ka ṭa ka ṇḍa a de ya* and consecrating with the *oṃkāra*, the elephants, the earth, and the [other elements] are thus conceived. The archways, cloths, bells, and chowries—[reciting] *oṃ sarvavit ṭha ā ṭha hoḥ*—one should form the vajrāñjali-muṣṭi mudrā, place it upon the maṇḍala, and offer the sacrifice.

[3] Having entered the maṇḍala and performed worship, one should recite the four-syllable mantra a thousand times. Having recited it while facing the deity of the maṇḍala, [one should perform] the rite for all purposes in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). The Blessed One [is present] in the maṇḍala... [the rest is blurred] ... [8] ... the supreme boon. Then the preceptor (ācārya) should ask as follows:
"O Great-Souled One, do you wish to receive the pure secret of the great family of Guhyakas?
Therefore, it should be said thus:
'I desire it.'"
Thus,
the preceptor, having explained the commitments (*samaya*) and the vows (*saṃvara*), should cause [the disciple] to take up the vows,
beginning with "I shall generate [them]" and continuing until "I shall establish sentient beings in cessation," provided that there is an acceptance of not transgressing them.
However, for one who does not take the vows, one should not say, "Today you must enter," and so forth; nor should the empowerment of the preceptor's authorization be performed.

Then, as before, having performed the dressing of the garments and so forth with the mantras for expelling the wicked and others, one should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) by means of the mantra:
*oṃ sarvayogacittam utpādayāmi*. Then, the vajra should be established in his heart by means of the heart-mantra.
Oṃ, you are the commitment of divine passion; Hoḥ! O Vajra, accomplish [this] as is pleasing.

Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas. You must not speak of this supreme secret maṇḍala of all the Tathāgatas to anyone who has not entered it, nor should it be treated with lack of faith.

Then, having bestowed the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon that disciple and having performed the ritual authorization (*pramāṇa*), one should empower him with the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*). Having sprinkled him with water from a jar placed outside and having placed the syllables *kha* and so forth on his head, one should armor him with the wrathful mudrā. Thus, with the pair of armors bound by the wrathful mudrās, and having caused him to take that very blue flower garland, one should lead him in until he enters. Having performed the summoning with the mantra beginning "Oṃ Vajradhara... and so forth, one should speak as follows: "O Great Passion, well-firm, well-pleased, well-faced; O Vajrasattva, grant me success today! One should then speak again as follows:

"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the vajra-knowledge by which you will attain even the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your *samaya* be violated. Having said this, he should form the entry-mudrā, place the vajra upon the head of the disciple, and speak thus:
This is your vow: if you should speak of this to anyone, it shall split your head with a vajra;
by that very same vow-water, [it shall be so].
Having visualized [the being] being filled by that [light], which has a radiance agitated by red flames, one should recite "HŪṂ AḤ" many times.

In this way, the entry of the being (*sattvāveśa*) occurs; then, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be bestowed upon him. Even for one who lacks wealth, when possessed, the accomplishment of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth will occur.
Having visualized a vajra on the tongue of the one possessed, one should say, "Speak, O Vajra!
He will then recount everything—past, future, and present, all as truth.

Then, one should release that mudrā upon the heart, [reciting]: "Stay, O Vajra! Be firm for me! Empower my heart! Grant me all accomplishments! HŪṂ HA HA HA HA HOḤ! In this way, one should make that possession firm.
Then, while casting that garland empowered by the syllable *TĀṂ* into the maṇḍala, he should speak thus:
"Accept it, O Vajra-hoḥ!
Then, wherever it falls, that [deity] will be accomplished for him.
Then, while binding that garland upon his head, one should speak thus:
"O being of great power, accept this worship!
Then, for one who has been thus possessed, one should release the binding of the mouth with this [mantra].
Oṃ!
Vajrasattva himself, intent today upon opening your eyes,
opens for you the unsurpassed vajra-eye, which is all-seeing.

"Behold the vajra! Having thus empowered the two eyes of the disciple with the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the midst of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), he should show him the mandala beginning with Padmavatī and ending with Vajradhara.

Then, proceeding toward the door of the trident on the outer mandala, he should draw a square mandala measuring the dimensions of the limbs of the mandala, with a western entrance and five colors; and in its center, an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp empowered by flames.

Having purified it like the root mandala, one should thereupon draw the Aparājita cloth-painting or a pedestal upon an elephant-throne; having placed it there after reciting the mantra for the expulsion of evil spirits, the preceptor—having made the disciple, who has offered the ritual fee and performed the *nirājana* rite, into the state of Vajradhara through auspicious rites and so forth, and having established him in his proper place with the six-limbed [protection] and other mantras and samaya-mudrās—should duly install him upon the Aparājita [image] using the Mahāmudrā in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.

Adorned above with white parasols and canopies consecrated by the recitation of the syllable *hūṃ*; with various garments, banners, and yak-tail whisks consecrated by the recitation of the syllable *oṃ*—
the Dharmas are clear, pure, and indeed unturbid.
Knowing that phenomena are thus ungraspable, ineffable, arisen from causes and karma, devoid of intrinsic nature, and untainted—
you have been born upon the breast of the Protectors to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings.
One should ring the bell produced from the final vowel according to that same method.
Then:
For existence is pure by its very nature;
by means of natures that are made non-existent, and by beings who are pure by nature, the supreme existence is brought about.

Then, having offered the bow and arrow with the syllable *hoḥ* and said, "To all the Tathāgatas," one should perform the gesture of discharging the bow and arrow in the four directions—one upward and the other downward.
Then, having placed the "Vajra-Cause"—that is, the Wheel of Dharma—between the feet, and the conch, which has the "Vajra-Speech" as its center, in the right hand, he should speak thus:
From this day forward, by the mere arising of the thought [of awakening], turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having completely filled the unsurpassed conch of Dharma in every direction,
you should, with a mind free from doubt or hesitation,
always proclaim in the world this method of the practice of mantra.
"Thus you sing that you are grateful to the Buddhas and a benefactor;
and all those Vajradharas shall protect you eternally.

Then, with the ego-identifications (*ahaṃkāra*) of Lokeśa, Ākāśagarbha, and so forth, in the forms of the Tathāgatas, Vajrasattva, and others, one should grant permission by means of five verses in succession.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, toward all beings in every way,
may the wheel of Dharma be turned throughout the universe according to their individual dispositions.
Thus, the four verses beginning with "Vajra, Krodha, Padma, Maṇi, Cakra" should be recited next.

Then, having bestowed the heart-mantra and taught the knowledge of the four mudrās according to the procedure for the means of accomplishment as spoken in the *Mantracodanabhāṣita*, and having placed the vajra in the hand of the disciple, one should make the prediction while forming the *udgatā* mudrā.
I, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva,
prophesy you for the sake of ultimate success in existence, having extracted you from the miserable states of rebirth.
"O Tathāgata named [Amuka]vajra, may you be accomplished; you are the pledge (samaya), bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ!
Holding the corner of the upper robe with the left hand in the *tathāgatamuṣṭi* (Tathāgata-fist) gesture, and extending the right hand in the *varada* (boon-granting) gesture—this is its mudrā.
Then, [10] the consolation of the assembly of all Tathāgatas and so forth should be bestowed.
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today completely liberated from all sins and are well-established.
There is no further death for you from this Great Bliss Vehicle;
invincible and unbound, rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.
The suffering of existence has ceased for you, so that ultimate liberation from existence may be achieved. This perfected commitment of the samaya must be constantly guarded by you.
This supreme and eternal command was proclaimed by all the Buddhas alike.
The bodhicitta must certainly not be abandoned, for it is the seal known as the vajra.
By the mere production of which one becomes a Buddha indeed, without a doubt;
that True Dharma must never be rejected nor ever abandoned.
Yet, out of ignorance or delusion, one might fail to reveal it.
One should not abandon one's own self nor afflict it with ascetic penances;
happiness should be maintained according to one's ease, for this one is the future Fully Awakened One.
The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā must never be abandoned.
The teacher must not be disparaged, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
Whoever should treat with contempt the teacher, the guru who is equal to all Buddhas,
shall constantly encounter suffering through the slighting of all Buddhas—
by means of fevers, poisons, toxins, diseases, disturbances caused by *ḍākinīs*, and planetary influences.
Slain by terrible obstacles and Vināyakas, he shall go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, [one should honor] the Vajrācārya, the great guru.
One should never despise someone whose excellent virtues are hidden.
Then, one should give a suitable gift to the preceptor along with a dakṣiṇā;
for thereafter, fevers and other afflictions no longer prevail.
One should always honor one's own master of the samaya even with one’s own life;
how much more so with sons, wives, and the like, which are not to be given away, let alone with unstable wealth?
For [the master] is always extremely difficult to find, even in tens of millions of incalculable eons.
It bestows Buddhahood upon one who possesses diligence in this very life;
what is given to him by all the Buddhas becomes eternal.
From that giving comes the accumulation of merit; from that accumulation comes supreme accomplishment.
One's own commitment must always be accomplished; likewise, the Tathāgatas must always be worshipped;
and one must always give to the guru, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
Today your birth has become fruitful, for you are well-established in this;
you will undoubtedly become equal to the deities of the Samaya.
Today, O long-lived ones, you have been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Vajrins.
The sovereign lords of the great kingdom of the three realms are steadfast;
having today utterly defeated the Māras, they have entered the supreme city.
"Buddhahood has been attained by you this very day; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having thus made this promise to the disciples, he pierced their right thumbs and grasped them with his left hand according to this rite.
Having offered one hundred oblations of clarified butter intended for the principal disciple,
he should offer one hundred oblations of sesame seeds mixed with honey, ghee, and curd.
Having sprinkled water around [the deity], touched his heart, and bound the *pratiśara* on his hand,
one should cause the Lord to perform a circumambulation and prostration while holding the parasol. Having entered through the eastern gate, one should speak these words once:
This disciple, having been thus informed, shall become a bearer of the tantra,
esteemed by the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the deities.
To him, this also should be said:

"For the sake of compassion for sentient beings, you must diligently draw the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure, and practitioners should be engaged in accordance with the tantra. Then, having offered the outer *bali* and performed the ritual ablution (*upaspṛśya*) as prescribed, he should address the disciples, saying, "All of you should perform worship according to your capacity. Having caused them to perform the worship and having satisfied those who entered [the maṇḍala] with all kinds of flavors, foods, and enjoyments dedicated to the Lord, he should offer the *argha* water to the Blessed One and, circumambulating the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure suitable for accomplishment, dismiss it.

Oṃ! Vajrasattva, maintain your pledge; abide as Vajrasattva. Be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be well-nourished by me, be devoted to me. Grant me all accomplishments and make my mind auspicious in all activities. Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become the Vajra! Great Samayasattva, Āḥ!

Having repeated this three times, one should recite: "Oṃ! Having delighted in the syllable *hūṃ*, one should dismiss the maṇḍala with the syllable *hūṃ*. Having cast the colored powders and the floral offerings into a great lake with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should uproot the stakes of the maṇḍala with the syllable *hūṃ* and wash them with milk. Then, having filled those pits with earth, one should perform a pacifying fire-offering (*śāntika-homa*) for oneself, one's disciples, and the king, according to the prescribed ritual."

Facing the *devatāpyāyana* [offering], there is a circular pit (*kuṇḍa*) one cubit in diameter, twelve finger-breadths deep at the bottom, and eight finger-breadths deep in the middle, marked with a five-pronged vajra. Above that, leaving an inner space of four finger-breadths, there is an altar (*vedī*) equal to it in width and height, marked with corner-vajras. Having smeared the pit all around on the outside with clay according to the ritual requirements, and having smeared it with fragrances appropriate to the rite, one should adorn it with loose flowers during the three junctions of the day. || O ||

The vessel is made of gold, copper, or wood such as *nimbā* or *icchika*. Its handle, ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, has a square face at the upper part; it contains a hollow two finger-breadths deep, encircled by a five-pronged vajra, with a channel for the flow of liquid in front measuring the width of the little finger. In the middle of the hollow, there is a three-pronged vajra four finger-breadths long. || 0 ||

The *sruva* ladle is shaped like a lotus petal, two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, with a hollow one finger-breadth deep, and a five-pronged vajra at its tip. Regarding the grasping of the vajra-fists for both [the *darvī* and the *sruva*], the handle is six finger-breadths below the vajra, which is a vajra-jewel. Thus, the *pātrī* and *sruva* are said to be the measure of a hand. ||o||

The *samidhs* (sacrificial fuel sticks) consist of *plakṣa*, *khadira*, *arka*, *nyagrodha*, *avaikaṅkata*, *tāmra*, *śamī*, *kāśyapa*, *apāmārga*, *aśvattha*, and *udumbara*. Each should be fresh, straight, and of excellent quality, measuring one *prādeśa* in length, with both ends sprinkled with fragrant water. These are to be offered in all ritual acts (*sarvakarma*). Whatever food is obtained, whether it be small or large, all of that should be offered daily with the utterance of *svāhā*, as well as regular *guggulu* resin. One should offer them separately according to the specific requirements of each rite.
And having recited the respective mantras according to the ritual action, one should present the offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth. || 0 ||

The section on oblations (*havya*). For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the fuel for sacrificial trees, *niṣka*, *kuṇḍa*, and cow dung [are used]. For rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should exclude wild cow dung and use all the aforementioned fuel as prescribed.

For malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*), one should use dry fuel from trees that are pungent, thorny, and foul-smelling, such as the *nimba* and *gardabheṣṭā* found in cremation grounds. For the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), one uses fuel from *nimba* and mango trees, as well as their flowers; indeed, for all rites, the fuel should correspond to the specific ritual action. || 0 ||

Then, having performed his ablutions, donned ornaments, and so forth, the mantra-practitioner should assume the identity of Vajradhara according to the specific rite. Seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or another suitable position, he should recite seven times over the previously mentioned *argha* water his own mantra, preceded and followed by *svāhā*. For all rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), having consecrated the vessel for all rites and the *argha* vessel with the "Expelling the Wicked" armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and mudrā, he should place them on his left side.

Having sprinkled the fuel sticks and other materials with water consecrated by those two [mantras] while holding it in the right hand, one should place the sacrificial offering (havya) on one's own right side; in the case of a cruel rite, the opposite should be done. The fire for a rite of pacification (śāntika) should be produced from a milky tree or from a forest fire, or from the fire of one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni).
Or from the kitchen of the Saṅgha for rites of pacification, nourishment, and subjugation;
or fire from the palace of a king or a nobleman, or fire from a forest conflagration or a kitchen, for the purpose of nourishment.
For a rite of wrath, the fire should be produced from a cremation ground, from bones, from stones, or from the house of a *caṇḍāla*;
for subjugation, it should be produced from the house of a prostitute or a merchant; and for attraction, the fire should be prepared by actors, wandering minstrels, or travelers.

Then, having separated the fire by means of the *duṣṭotsāraṇa* mantra, and having sprinkled it three times with water consecrated by that same mantra while holding it with the tips of *kuśa* grass, one should add clean, well-dried grass and kindle it with the wind from a fan.
The mantra is: *oṃ jvala 2 hūṃ*.
One should cause it to blaze up with ghee over which the syllable *hūṃ* has been recited seven times.

Then, having recited "Oṃ Vajrasattva Āḥ," one should place upon the altar—facing east and so forth—a blade of *kuśa* grass that has been consecrated by this mantra; it should be fresh, stainless, with unbroken leaves, of uniform green color, neither too long nor too short. One should then cover the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with these *kuśa* blades, their tips pointing toward the east.

Then, having produced the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the syllable *HŪṂ*, and having produced within it—on the lotus in the center of the eight-spoked diagram (*śṛṅgāṭaka*)—the fire arising from the syllable *RUṂ* according to the specific ritual action; and having performed the rites of summoning and so forth for the fire situated in the pit using the mantras beginning with *OṂ VAJRADHARA*; and having expelled the malevolent spirits and performed the armor-visualization (*kavaca*) and the binding of the directions (*digbandha*); and having offered the water of honor (*argha*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*) to the fire with its mantra as before;
and having visualized [the fire] at the end of its own mantra and said, *JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ SAMAYASTHA SAMAYAS TVAM*; one should recite three times: *OṂ AGNAYE SVĀHĀ*.

Having performed the establishment of the seal-consecration (*mudrābhiṣeka*) and the pledge (*samaya*) as before, and having bound the armor-seal (*kavacamudrā*), one should command: "Perform this! Then, knowing one's own [authority], and having worshipped with offerings such as perfume according to the ritual action—using the fourfold worship beginning with Umā—and having expelled the malevolent ones, one sprinkles water three times around [the site].

With the thumb of the right fist, having mentally internalized the *bodhicitta*—which has been fashioned from the tip of one's own index finger, together with a mustard-seed mandala and a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth—and having recollected the *bodhicitta* in the form of non-arising within the heart, and having empowered it at the heart-center of one’s own samaya, one should bind the armor as before. Then, having arisen, one should perform the rites for the *caitya* and so forth. In this manner, it should be practiced every day during the four sessions.

In that regard, first, according to the previously stated method, one should recite each of the six-limbed mantras and the vajra-flames individually two hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). Then, one should recite the Bhagavat until a sign (*nimitta*) is obtained. Afterwards, one should accomplish the desired siddhis, such as pills, collyrium, foot-ointment, invisibility, the sword, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), and sandals; as well as other siddhis, including killing, expulsion, hatred, delusion, subjugation, reviving the dead, changing form, treasure-finding, and mastery over hosts of spirits.
Thus ends the sādhana of the Blessed Lord Śrī Bhūtaḍāmara Bhaṭṭāraka, whose *hūṃ* sounds are as terrible and deep as the roar of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
This procedure is for those who possess knowledge of the true nature of ritual injunctions,
so that men who practice it without interruption may achieve various kinds of success.
Without doubt, Subhūtipālita has uttered these words.

This is the work of the great scholar, the great maṇḍala-ācārya, the venerable Subhūtipālita. [It contains] the Ritual for Preliminary Service and the Genealogy of Kings. Samvat [year], day 17. This manuscript belongs to the monk Śīlākaragupta.
